claim: Chinco, Clark-Joseph and Ye (Journal of Finance 74(1), 2019): rolling 30-minute LASSO on the lagged 1-minute returns of all NYSE stocks forecasts the next minute; out-of-sample R2 rises by at least 1.2 percentage points and the forecast-implied strategy has an annualized Sharpe ratio of 1.8 net of trading costs; TAQ 2005-2012, 250 random stocks a day, price >= $5, trading only when the forecast exceeds the bid-ask spread.
impact_on_spec: Source of the LASSO cross-sectional design and of the rule 'trade only when the forecast exceeds the spread' (our k filter). Horizon is 1 minute; ours is 15-60 minutes, so the claim is not transferred, only the method.
independent_replication: Aït-Sahalia et al. 2022 find predictability across all stocks but vanishing within about five minutes; no independent replication at 15-60 minutes found.
limitations: 1-minute horizon; costs are one bid-ask spread per trade at the mid, not a measured fill; 2005-2012 decimal-era US data before the current auction/ATS structure; the paper itself says the naive strategy ignores trading costs and adds a spread filter.
quote: increases both out-of-sample fit and forecast-implied Sharpe ratios, and we show that

claim: The authors state the naive LASSO-implied strategy 'ignores trading costs ... which are substantial when trading at the 1-minute horizon', and fix it by executing only when the forecast exceeds the bid-ask spread and charging the spread on realized returns.
impact_on_spec: Direct basis of the k filter (trade only when the predicted return exceeds k times the one-side cost) and of reporting costs separately.
limitations: Spread-only cost model; no market-impact or fee model.

claim: Aït-Sahalia, Fan, Xue and Zhou (NBER w30366, Management Science): machine-learning predictability of high-frequency stock returns is large and pervasive at ultra short horizons, but a binary direction forecast becomes no better than a coin toss in just five minutes (about 2,000 transactions), and about 80% of the predictability comes from the most recent 10 milliseconds.
impact_on_spec: Warns that the published ML predictability is a millisecond-to-minute phenomenon; at 15-60 minutes the model has to find a different, slower source. The contract therefore treats a null as the prior.
independent_replication: Consistent with Chinco et al. (1-minute) and with the cost survey I-20261006-01.
limitations: Tick-level quote/trade features not available in 5-minute bars; the paper values latency, which a retail Alpaca account cannot buy.
quote: no better than a coin toss) in just five minutes

claim: Baltussen, Da and Soebhag (2025): stocks that lost the most from the previous close to 15:00 (ROD3) rise in the last 30 minutes; 1993-2019 low-minus-high quintile spread is 3.78 bp/day (value-weighted) and 6.86 bp/day (equal-weighted), t of 10.6 and 17.3; the authors write that after transaction costs the strategy as presented might not be exploitable by many investors.
impact_on_spec: Baseline B1 (end-of-day reversal). Note the paper's sort return is previous close to 15:00 and the hold is 15:30-16:00; the contract's baseline sorts at 15:30 on the open-to-15:30 return as the owner specified, a disclosed variant.
independent_replication: Quantpedia Awards 2025 second place (not a replication); local T-13 and I-20261006-01 found the closing-window cross-section untested net of measured costs.
limitations: Gross returns; the authors do not net costs; sample ends 2019 so our 2024-2026 data are a true out-of-sample test.
quote: 6.86 bps per day, or 17.3% a year, for the equal-weighted L-S

claim: Heston, Korajczyk and Sadka (Journal of Finance 2010): the return of a half-hour interval predicts returns at the same half-hour on later days; the top-minus-bottom decile spread is 3.01 bp at the same time on the next day, comparable to twice the quoted half-spread of S&P 500 stocks (1.7 bp in 2008), so it is of the order of costs.
independent_replication: Lou, Polk and Skouras 2019 (half-hour components); local t20260930_13 intraday periodicity run.
limitations: 2001-2005 data; the authors compare with the spread and do not show a net strategy; our own T-13 test (t20260930_13) found net losses.
quote: winners and the bottom decile of losers is 3.01 basis points at the same time on the next day.

claim: Ballarin, Capra and Dellaportas (arXiv 2504.19623): ridge-readout echo state networks forecast the cross-section of S&P 500 stock returns at 10-minute steps; random forest is worse than the linear baseline by about the same absolute margin as the ESN gains, MSFE reductions are at most 0.87%, and a 10-minute mean-variance portfolio shows the best gross Sharpe and the lowest transaction costs among the compared forecasts.
impact_on_spec: The only published cross-sectional stock ML at a horizon near ours; shows that tree models did not beat ridge, so the contract keeps a ridge/LASSO baseline and requires LightGBM to beat it.
limitations: Preprint; MSFE gains below 1%; the economic evaluation is a single mean-variance portfolio with its own cost assumption; no placebo; sample not matched to our window.

claim: Alpaca paper trading fills every order against the NBBO with random partial fills 10% of the time and no depth check, so paper fills are optimistic for multi-name intraday books.
impact_on_spec: The paper sleeve of this task would trade market orders on 10-60 minute cycles; paper cannot validate impact, so the model cost stays the binding estimate.
quote: all orders submitted in paper trading will be matched against the best available current market price (NBBO)

claim: SEC Section 31 fee is $20.60 per million of covered sales on or after 2026-04-04, i.e. 0.206 bp of sell value.
impact_on_spec: The 0.2 bp sell-side fee in the cost model of this contract.
independent_replication: Alpaca fee schedule quoted in I-20261006-01 section 4.
limitations: Before 2026-04-04 the fee was $0 per million; the contract charges 0.2 bp on every sale over the whole window, a small conservative simplification.
